text: [[astronomer|Astronomers]] in ancient and [[medieval|medieval]] India made careful observations of the sky and built mathematical systems to predict the movements of the Sun, Moon and planets. They worked out the length of the year very precisely, predicted eclipses and developed new tools in mathematics to do it.

The best-known is [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]]. In 499 CE, aged 23, he wrote the Aryabhatiya. In it, he said the Earth spins on its [[axis|axis]], explained [[eclipse|eclipses]] as shadows rather than demons, and gave pi as 3.1416. Later astronomers, like Brahmagupta, [[@bhaskara|Bhaskara II]] and the scholars of Kerala, added much more.
Indian astronomy also learned from, and taught, other cultures, including Greek, Persian and Arab astronomers.

Aryabhata said the Earth spins on its axis, which was a bold idea. But in his system the Sun and planets still moved around the Earth. The idea of the Earth orbiting the Sun was argued in Europe by Copernicus about a thousand years later.

sec.t:
The oldest Indian astronomy grew out of keeping time for [[ritual|rituals]] and farming. A text called the Vedanga Jyotisha gives rules for a calendar based on the Sun and Moon. Scholars disagree about its age, with estimates spread across several centuries in the first millennium BCE.

Ancient Indian astronomers divided the Moon's path across the sky into 27 parts, called nakshatras or lunar mansions. Each night, the Moon sits in a different one, and each has a name, like Ashwini or Rohini. Rohini's brightest star is the orange giant that Western astronomers call Aldebaran, the eye of the bull in Taurus. These names are still used in Indian calendars, festivals and family traditions today.

Aryabhata worked near Pataliputra, close to today's [[@bihar-history|Patna]]. In just 121 verses, the Aryabhatiya covered mathematics and astronomy.

He wrote that the stars seem to move westwards because the Earth turns, like a person in a boat who sees the trees on the bank moving backwards. Most thinkers of his time, in India and elsewhere, believed the Earth stood still. He described lunar and solar [[@eclipses|eclipses]] as shadows, and he estimated the Earth's size with good accuracy.

In 1975, India named its first satellite after him.

sec.h: Brahmagupta, Bhaskara and the Kerala school
sec.t:
In 628 CE, [[@brahmagupta|Brahmagupta]] wrote a large book on astronomy that included the earliest known rules for calculating with [[@zero-to-computers|zero]] and [[@negative-numbers|negative numbers]]. He also wrote that objects fall towards the Earth because it attracts them, though he did not have a theory of [[gravity|gravity]] like Newton's.

Around 1150, Bhaskara II wrote the Siddhanta Shiromani, which was studied for centuries. From the 14th to the 16th century, scholars in Kerala, starting with [[@madhava|Madhava]], found new ways to calculate pi and the positions of planets. Around 1500, Nilakantha Somayaji described a system in which the five visible planets circle the Sun, while the Sun circles the Earth. A Danish astronomer, Tycho Brahe, proposed something similar about 90 years later.

Astronomy in India did not grow alone. Varahamihira, in the 6th century, summarised five astronomical systems, including two linked to Greek and Roman ideas. In the 8th century, Indian astronomical texts were translated into Arabic in Baghdad. Through Arab scholars, Indian numerals, including zero, eventually reached Europe.

Historians enjoy tracing these links, though they don't always agree on who learned what from whom. Some popular claims that ancient texts predicted modern discoveries in detail are not supported by experts. What is well documented is impressive enough: careful observation, clever mathematics and a long tradition that ran from Pataliputra to Ujjain, Kerala and the stone instruments of [[@jantar-mantar|Jantar Mantar]].

sec.h: खेत का लड़का, जिसने ग्रह खोजा
sec.t:
क्लाइड टॉमबॉ अमेरिका के कंसास में एक खेत पर पले-बढ़े। अपनी [[@telescopes-how|दूरबीनें]] भी उन्होंने खुद बनाईं। उनसे मंगल और बृहस्पति को देखकर जो चित्र बनाए, वे उन्होंने लोवेल वेधशाला भेज दिए। 1929 में वेधशाला ने उन्हें नौकरी दे दी। तब उनकी उम्र 22 साल थी और उनके पास कॉलेज की कोई डिग्री नहीं थी।

काम बड़े धीरज का था। वे आसमान के एक ही हिस्से की तस्वीरें कुछ रातों के अंतर पर खींचते, फिर एक खास मशीन में दोनों तस्वीरों को बार-बार अदल-बदलकर देखते। तारे अपनी जगह टिके रहते हैं। जो चीज़ खिसकती दिखे, वह ग्रह हो सकती है। महीनों की खोज के बाद, 18 फ़रवरी 1930 को, उन्हें एक धुँधला-सा बिंदु उछलता दिखा। तब से अब तक प्लूटो ने सूरज का एक चक्कर भी पूरा नहीं किया है। उसका पहला चक्कर 2178 में पूरा होगा।

sec.t:
1990 के दशक से खगोलशास्त्रियों को प्लूटो वाले इलाके में ही सैकड़ों बर्फ़ीले पिंड मिलने लगे। अब इस इलाके को काइपर बेल्ट कहते हैं। 2005 में एरिस मिला। वह चौड़ाई में लगभग प्लूटो जितना है, और उसका [[mass|द्रव्यमान]] प्लूटो से ज़्यादा है।

अब फ़ैसला करना ज़रूरी हो गया। या तो एरिस और शायद ऐसे दर्जनों पिंड भी ग्रह कहलाते, या फिर प्लूटो को कुछ और मानना पड़ता। 2006 में प्राग में खगोलशास्त्रियों ने वोट डाला और दूसरा रास्ता चुना। यह फ़ैसला इतना मशहूर हुआ कि अमेरिकन डायलेक्ट सोसाइटी ने “प्लूटोड” (plutoed) को 2006 का ‘साल का शब्द’ चुना। इसका मतलब है, किसी का दर्जा घटा देना।

कुछ वैज्ञानिकों को यह नियम ठीक नहीं लगता। न्यू होराइज़न्स मिशन के प्रमुख एलन स्टर्न कहते हैं कि जो भी चीज़ इतनी बड़ी हो कि अपने ही खिंचाव से गेंद जैसी गोल हो जाए, उसे ग्रह मानना चाहिए। इस हिसाब से तो प्लूटो पक्का ग्रह है। उस पर पहाड़ हैं, मौसम है, धुँधला आसमान है और पाँच चाँद हैं। दूसरे वैज्ञानिक कहते हैं कि “रास्ता साफ़ करने” वाली शर्त सौरमंडल को समझने का अच्छा तरीका है। यह बहस अभी चल ही रही है।

न्यू होराइज़न्स 2006 में रवाना हुआ, उसी साल जब प्लूटो का दर्जा बदला गया। साढ़े नौ साल के सफ़र के बाद, जुलाई 2015 में वह प्लूटो के पास से गुज़रा। उसने वहाँ अमेरिका के रॉकी पहाड़ों जितने ऊँचे, पानी की बर्फ़ से बने पहाड़ देखे, नीली धुंध देखी, और दिल के आकार का एक विशाल इलाका देखा। इस इलाके का नाम अब टॉमबॉ रेजियो है। इसका बायाँ आधा हिस्सा जमी हुई नाइट्रोजन का एक बहुत बड़ा मैदान है, जिसे स्पुतनिक प्लैनिशिया कहते हैं। क्लाइड टॉमबॉ की अस्थियों का थोड़ा-सा हिस्सा भी इस यान के साथ सफ़र पर गया।

प्लूटो का सबसे बड़ा चाँद शैरन, प्लूटो से लगभग आधा चौड़ा है। दोनों एक-दूसरे के चारों ओर ऐसे घूमते हैं जैसे हाथ पकड़कर नाचते दो दोस्त। प्लूटो लगभग 2,380 किलोमीटर चौड़ा है, यानी हमारे अपने चाँद से भी छोटा। देखो कि वह [[@planets-size|ग्रहों]] के सामने कितना छोटा है, या उसके बर्फ़ीले पड़ोसियों, [[@comets|धूमकेतुओं]] से मिलो।

text: A lotus leaf looks smooth, but it isn't. Under a [[@microscopes|microscope]], its surface is covered in tiny bumps, each far thinner than a hair. The bumps are coated with even smaller crystals of wax.

Water hates wax, and it can't settle into the spaces between the bumps. So a raindrop sits on the very tips of the bumps, with pockets of air underneath. It pulls itself into a ball and rolls off at the slightest tilt. A surface this good at shedding water is called [[superhydrophobic|superhydrophobic]], meaning "very afraid of water".
As the drops roll, dust and dirt stick to them and are carried away. So the lotus, rising out of muddy water, keeps its leaves spotless. Scientists call this the lotus effect.

sec.t:
On a smooth surface, a water drop spreads out and dirt stays stuck. On the lotus leaf, dirt only touches the tips of the bumps, so it barely holds on. The rolling drops collect it easily.

This matters for the plant. A clean leaf catches more sunlight to make food. Dirt and [[fungus|fungus]] spores get washed away before they can cause disease. The lotus is even unusual in having its breathing pores on the top of its leaves, which would be a problem if water stayed sitting there.

The lotus grows in ponds and lakes across Asia. Its roots creep through the mud at the bottom, while its leaves and flowers rise on long stalks well above the water. Water lilies look similar, but their leaves and flowers usually float flat on the surface.

Lotus flowers can even warm themselves. On cool days, the flower keeps its centre at around 30 to 35°C, which may attract insects looking for a cosy place to rest.

Almost every part of the lotus is useful. The crunchy stems, called kamal kakdi or bhein, are cooked as vegetables. The seeds are eaten raw or roasted. The leaves are used as plates in some places.

Because it rises clean and beautiful out of mud, the lotus has long stood for purity. In Hindu art, the goddesses Lakshmi and Saraswati are often shown seated on a lotus. In Buddhism, it represents a mind rising above the troubles of the world, and the [[@buddha|Buddha]] is often pictured on a lotus throne. Jain art uses it too.

The lotus is India's national flower, one of its [[@national-symbols|national symbols]]. In [[@delhi|Delhi]], the Bahá'í House of Worship, opened in 1986, is shaped like a white lotus with 27 marble petals and is known as the [[@modern-architecture|Lotus Temple]].

Lotus seeds have very tough coats. In the 1990s, an American scientist, Jane Shen-Miller, planted lotus seeds from a dried-up lake bed in northeast China. Tests showed one was about 1,300 years old, the oldest seed known at that time to grow into a healthy plant.

Lotus ponds are under pressure from drainage and pollution in many places. Protecting [[@wetlands|wetlands]] protects the lotus, and the frogs, fish and birds that live among its leaves.

text: When a truck drives onto a bridge, its weight pushes down. The bridge has to carry that weight to the ground at each end, or to pillars in between, without bending too much or breaking.

Engineers think about two forces. **Compression** squeezes things together, like stacking heavy books on a box. **Tension** stretches things apart, like a rope in a tug-of-war. Stone and concrete are good at being squeezed but crack when pulled. Steel cables are superb at being pulled but would crumple if squashed. Every bridge design is a way of sending the load through the parts that can handle it.
Lay a ruler across two cups and press the middle. The top surface gets squeezed and the bottom gets stretched. That is a beam bridge in miniature.

myth: Bridges are solid and don't move at all.

Bridges are designed to flex. Steel grows longer on hot days and shorter on cold ones, so bridges have expansion joints, the metal teeth you feel as a bump when you drive over them. Long suspension bridges can also sway several metres sideways in strong winds.

sec.t:
The simplest bridge is a beam, a log across a stream. It works for short gaps but sags if made too long.

Arches are much stronger. An arch turns the weight pressing down into a sideways push that travels around the curve into the ground. Roman engineers built stone arch bridges and [[aqueduct|aqueducts]], some still standing after 2,000 years, as you can see alongside [[@roman-roads|Roman roads]].

Truss bridges use frames of triangles. A triangle can't change shape unless one of its sides breaks, which makes it the stiffest simple shape there is. Many old railway bridges across Indian rivers are steel trusses, criss-crossed with diagonal beams. As a train rolls over one, some beams are squeezed and others are stretched, and the triangles share the load between them.

[[@howrah-bridge|The Howrah Bridge]] over the Hooghly in [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] is a cantilever bridge. It is built from two huge steel arms reaching out from each bank and joined in the middle. It opened in 1943 and is held together with rivets, not nuts and bolts. Tens of thousands of vehicles and many more people on foot cross it every day.

In Jammu and Kashmir, [[@india-wonder-chenab-bridge|the Chenab Rail Bridge]] is a steel arch about 359 metres above the river, higher than the [[@eiffel-tower|Eiffel Tower]] is tall. It opened to trains in 2025, after nearly two decades of work in the mountains.

In [[@meghalaya|Meghalaya]], in [[@northeast-india|northeast India]], Khasi and Jaintia communities have trained the roots of rubber fig trees across streams for generations. Over many years, the roots thicken and twist into living bridges. Some are strong enough to carry dozens of people at once, and they get stronger as the trees grow.

Bridges can fail when engineers misjudge a force. In 1940, the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in the US state of Washington twisted wildly in a steady wind and collapsed four months after opening. Nobody died, and engineers have tested bridge designs in wind tunnels ever since.

sec.t:
रहमान का जन्म 1967 में मद्रास में हुआ, जिसे अब [[@chennai|चेन्नई]] कहते हैं। तब उनका नाम ए.एस. दिलीप कुमार था। उनके पिता आर.के. शेखर [[@malayalam|मलयालम]] और तमिल फ़िल्मों में संगीत सजाते और वादकों का संचालन करते थे। नन्हा दिलीप कीबोर्ड पर उनके पास बैठा रहता।

नौ साल की उम्र में उनके पिता गुज़र गए। पैसे कमाने के लिए परिवार ने पिता के वाद्य किराए पर देने शुरू किए। किशोर उम्र में दिलीप फ़िल्मी संगीतकारों के लिए कीबोर्ड बजाने लगे, जिनमें मशहूर इलैयाराजा भी थे। साथ ही उन्होंने [[@classical-western|पश्चिमी शास्त्रीय संगीत]] सीखा। बीस-बाईस की उम्र में उन्होंने और उनके परिवार ने सूफ़ी इस्लाम अपनाया, और उन्होंने अल्लाह रक्खा रहमान नाम रखा।

1992 में निर्देशक मणिरत्नम ने उनसे *रोजा* का संगीत बनाने को कहा। गाने ताज़ा और साफ़ सुनाई देते थे, उनकी [[rhythm|लय]] में खनकते ढोल-ड्रम थे और अनोखी आवाज़ें थीं। गाने खूब चले, पहले तमिल में और फिर हिंदी में डब होकर।

फिर हिंदी फ़िल्में आईं: *रंगीला*, *दिल से*, जिसका गाना *छैयाँ छैयाँ* चलती ट्रेन की छत पर फ़िल्माया गया, *ताल* और *लगान*। उनके संगीत में [[@carnatic-hindustani|कर्नाटक संगीत]], सूफ़ी गायकी और लोकगीत थे, और साथ में [[@hip-hop|हिप-हॉप]] और [[@electronic-music|इलेक्ट्रॉनिक बीट]] भी। 1997 में भारत की आज़ादी के पचास साल पूरे होने पर उन्होंने *वंदे मातरम्* एल्बम निकाला, जिसमें *माँ तुझे सलाम* गाना था।

2008 में ब्रिटिश निर्देशक डैनी बॉयल ने [[@mumbai|मुंबई]] की कहानी पर *स्लमडॉग मिलियनेयर* बनाई और रहमान से संगीत देने को कहा। 2009 के अकादमी अवॉर्ड में उन्होंने सबसे अच्छे मूल संगीत का ऑस्कर जीता, और गीतकार गुलज़ार के साथ *जय हो* के लिए सबसे अच्छे मूल गीत का भी।

इसके बाद उन्होंने ब्रिटेन और [[@hollywood|हॉलीवुड]] की फ़िल्मों और मंच के शो के लिए संगीत दिया। इससे पहले वे *बॉम्बे ड्रीम्स* का संगीत भी बना चुके थे, जो लंदन में एंड्रयू लॉयड वेबर का बनाया एक [[@broadway|संगीत-नाटक]] था।

[[pitch|सुरीली]] धुनें गढ़ने के उनके हुनर की वजह से लोग रहमान को कभी-कभी "मद्रास का मोत्ज़ार्ट" कहते हैं, यानी [[@mozart|मोत्ज़ार्ट]] से उनकी तुलना करते हैं। इंटरव्यू में वे शांत और शर्मीले रहते हैं, और पुरस्कार जीतने पर ऊपरवाले का शुक्रिया अदा करना नहीं भूलते।

2008 में उन्होंने चेन्नई में केएम म्यूज़िक कंज़र्वेटरी खोली, जहाँ नौजवान संगीतकार भारतीय और पश्चिमी, दोनों तरह का संगीत सीखते हैं। उनके गाने सुनकर बड़े हुए कई संगीतकार कहते हैं कि रहमान ने उन्हें दिखाया कि भारतीय फ़िल्मी संगीत कहीं से भी विचार ले सकता है और फिर भी भारतीय ही सुनाई देता है। [[@bollywood-music|बॉलीवुड के गानों]] की कहानी में उनका काम एक बड़ा अध्याय है।

text: The Election Commission of India is the independent body that [[@elections-india|runs elections]] for the [[@lok-sabha-rajya-sabha|Lok Sabha]], the Rajya Sabha, state assemblies, and the offices of President and Vice-President. It keeps the list of voters, sets the dates, supervises every polling station and announces the results.

Article 324 of the [[@constitution|Constitution]] gives it its powers. Until 1989 it had just one member. Today it has a Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners. During an election, crores of government employees, teachers and police officers work under its orders. Its job is to make sure every eligible citizen can vote freely and that every vote counts the same. Elections to village councils and town bodies are run separately by each state's own election commission.

st.reveal: Machines were first tried in 1982 in part of the Paravur seat in Kerala. They were used more and more in state elections in the late 1990s, and in 2004 every Lok Sabha seat used them.

sec.h: The ink that won't wash off
sec.t: Since 1962, the ink painted on voters' left index fingers has come from Mysore Paints and Varnish, a company in [[@mysuru|Mysuru]] once owned by the Maharaja of Mysore. The [[@ink|ink]] contains silver nitrate, which reacts with skin and light to leave a dark mark that lasts for days or weeks. It stops anyone voting twice. The company also sends the ink to elections in many other countries.

Once elections are announced, a Model Code of Conduct comes into force. Governments can't announce new schemes to win votes, ministers can't use official cars for campaigning, and parties shouldn't appeal for votes on the basis of religion or caste. Campaigning must stop 48 hours before polling.

The code was rarely enforced strictly until T. N. Seshan became Chief Election Commissioner in 1990. He cracked down on illegal posters, overspending and the misuse of government machinery, and became famous across India for it. Politicians complained that he was too strict. Many voters loved him for exactly the same reason, and later commissioners kept many of his rules.

For decades, Indians voted by stamping paper ballots, which then had to be counted by hand for days. Electronic voting machines were tried in 1982 in Kerala, and in 2004 every Lok Sabha seat used them. Each one runs on a battery, so it works in villages without electricity. The machines are not connected to the internet, and they are stored under guard between polling day and counting day.

Since 2019, every machine has been paired with a VVPAT printer, which shows the voter a paper slip of their choice. Some parties and activists have questioned whether the machines can be trusted. The Commission and the Supreme Court have examined these concerns. So far the courts have upheld the system, while ordering paper slips to be checked against machine counts at some polling stations in every seat.

text: Researchers who study happiness keep finding the same big ingredients: warm relationships with family and friends, good health, enough money to feel safe, and a sense that your life has purpose. Feeling free to make your own choices, and living in a fair, trusting community, matter too.

Some things matter less than people expect. Extra money makes a big difference when a family is poor. Once people are comfortable, each extra rupee or dollar adds less. Fame and new possessions give a quick lift that soon fades. [[gene|Genes]] play a part too, which is why some people seem naturally cheerful.

st.prompt: In a famous 1978 study, people who had won big lottery prizes were asked how happy they were. What did researchers find?

options.t: They weren't much happier than people who hadn't won
They were far happier for the rest of their lives
They were much unhappier than everyone else

st.reveal: A year or so after the win, the winners were not much happier than people who hadn't won, and enjoyed small everyday pleasures less. People get used to good and bad changes surprisingly fast. Psychologists call this adaptation.

sec.h: The study that has lasted a lifetime

sec.t:
People are good at adjusting. A new bicycle feels wonderful for a few weeks, then it's just your bicycle. Psychologists call this hedonic [[adaptation|adaptation]]. A 1978 study found that lottery winners, after a while, were not much happier than people who hadn't won.

This is one reason some psychologists suggest spending on experiences, like a family trip or learning to swim, more than on things. Studies by Thomas Gilovich at Cornell University found that people often stay happier about experiences for longer. Memories of a trip can even grow fonder with time, and they are usually shared with other people.

It works the other way too. People often recover from setbacks better than they expect. That doesn't mean bad things don't hurt. It means our feelings tend to drift back towards our usual level over time.

Every year, the World Happiness Report asks people in more than 140 countries to picture a ladder from 0 to 10. The top is the best possible life for them, the bottom the worst. Then it asks which step they're on now.

In 2026, Finland came top for the ninth year running, and India ranked 116th. Nordic countries do well partly because people trust each other and their governments, and have good support when things go wrong. [[@bhutan|Bhutan]], a small Himalayan kingdom, took a different path: in the 1970s its king said "Gross National Happiness" was more important than national income, and the country still surveys its people's wellbeing.

Scientists have tested everyday habits that seem to lift mood. Spending time with [[@friendship|friends]], getting enough sleep and moving your body all help. So does time outdoors among trees or water. Doing something kind for someone else often makes the helper feel good too, a finding studied in [[@kindness-science|the science of kindness]].

In 2018, Delhi's government schools added a daily "Happiness Class", where children talk about feelings, practise paying attention and do activities about helping others. Many schools in the USA run similar social and emotional learning lessons.

Feeling sad, angry or worried sometimes is a normal part of being human. Happiness isn't about feeling great all the time. If sadness hangs around for weeks, though, it's worth talking to a parent, teacher or doctor, just as you would about a pain that won't go away.

text: To become an airline pilot, you need to learn to fly, pass written exams, pass a strict medical check, and build up hundreds of hours in the air. In India, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) gives out the Commercial Pilot Licence. You must be at least 18, have studied physics and maths up to Class 12, and have flown about 200 hours.
That licence lets you be paid to fly, but it is only the start. Airlines then train new pilots on the exact plane they will fly, mostly in simulators, before they ever carry passengers.

st.prompt: Before they ever fly a new airliner with passengers, where do pilots practise emergencies like an engine failure?

options.t: In a full flight simulator on the ground
On a real plane with passengers, but very carefully
Only in books and classroom lessons

st.reveal: Airline pilots train in full flight simulators, life-size copies of the cockpit that tilt and shake on hydraulic legs. Instructors can set off fires, storms and engine failures that would be far too dangerous to practise in a real plane.

myth: You need perfect eyesight to become a pilot.
Many airline pilots wear glasses or contact lenses. What matters is that your vision, with correction, meets the medical standard, and that you can see colours properly.

sec.t:
Most pilots begin in a small plane with one [[propeller|propeller]] and two seats, with an instructor beside them. The first lessons are about the basics: taking off, turning, climbing and, above all, landing. After about 10 to 20 hours of lessons, many students fly their first solo, alone in the plane for a few minutes. Pilots often remember that day for the rest of their lives. By tradition in some flying schools, a student's shirt tail is cut off after the first solo and pinned to the wall with the date.

Students also study weather, [[navigation|navigation]], radio calls, engines and the science of [[@airplanes-fly|how planes fly]]. They take exams in each subject. In India, a student pilot can start training at 16.

An airliner has two pilots: a captain on the left and a first officer on the right. They take turns flying and keep checking each other. Before every flight they study the weather, decide how much fuel to carry and walk around the plane looking for problems.

Much of the cruising is done by the autopilot, but pilots are always watching, talking to [[@air-traffic|air traffic controllers]] and ready to take over. Takeoff and landing are usually flown by hand, or closely watched if the plane lands itself in fog. Long-haul pilots may cross several time zones in a day and have to manage tiredness carefully.

Pilots must pass a medical check every year, and more often as they get older. Doctors test their eyes, hearing, heart and blood pressure. In most countries, airline pilots must retire at 65. Every six months or so, airline pilots go back to the simulator to practise emergencies and pass a test again. Pilots also have strict limits on how many hours they can fly in a day, a week and a month, so that a tired crew is never at the controls.

In 1936, [[@hist-first-woman-pilot-india|Sarla Thakral]] became the first Indian woman to earn a pilot's licence. Today India has a higher share of women airline pilots than most countries: more than one in ten pilots in India are women, compared with about one in twenty worldwide (2020s figures).

The first licence in India went to J.R.D. Tata in 1929. In 1932 he flew a small plane carrying mail from Karachi to Bombay, the first flight of the airline that later became Air India. Every pilot who takes off from an Indian [[@airports|airport]] today follows that route into the sky.

text: India's laws are made by [[@lok-sabha-rajya-sabha|Parliament]], which has two houses: the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. A proposed law is called a bill. Most bills must be passed by both houses and signed by the President before they become an Act, the official name for a law.
Along the way, a bill is read, debated, sent to committees, changed and voted on. Members can argue about every line.
Courts make sure new laws follow the Constitution. Even after a law is passed, anyone can challenge it in court if they think it breaks people's rights.

events.d: A proposed law, called a bill, is written and introduced in Parliament.
Members elected by the people debate it, suggest changes and vote.
The other house of Parliament, mostly chosen by the states, debates and votes too.
The President gives approval, called assent. Now it's a law!
If people think a law breaks the Constitution, courts can check it.

quiz.reveal: Only 14 private members' bills have ever become law in India, and the last was in 1970. Most laws today are proposed by the government, which controls much of Parliament's time. Private bills still matter, because they can push ideas into public debate.

sec.t:
The Lok Sabha, or House of the People, has 543 members elected directly by voters. [[@elections-india|Elections are held every five years]].

The Rajya Sabha, or Council of States, can have up to 250 members. Most are elected by members of the state assemblies, and the President nominates up to 12 people known for their work in art, science, literature or social service. The Rajya Sabha is never [[dissolve|dissolved]]. A third of its members retire every two years.

Since 2023, both houses have met in a new [[@parliament-india|Parliament]] building in New Delhi.

Sometimes the two houses can't agree. The Constitution then allows a joint sitting, where members of both meet together and vote. Because the Lok Sabha is bigger, it usually wins. This has happened only three times, most recently in 2002.

Money bills, about taxes and spending, are different. They can only start in the Lok Sabha, and the Rajya Sabha can only suggest changes within 14 days.

[[parliament|Parliament]] does more than pass laws. In Question Hour, MPs ask ministers questions, and ministers must answer, which keeps the government on its toes. Debates are shown live on Sansad TV, so anyone can watch.

The presiding officer keeps order: the Speaker in the Lok Sabha and the Vice-President of India, who chairs the Rajya Sabha. When debates get heated, they can suspend members or adjourn the house.

Once both houses pass a bill, it goes to the President for assent, meaning approval. For most bills, the President can send it back once and ask Parliament to think again. If Parliament passes it a second time, the President must sign.

Parliament doesn't make every law. The Constitution splits subjects into three lists. Parliament handles things like defence and railways. State assemblies handle things like police and farming. Both can make laws on shared subjects, like education, but if they clash, Parliament's law usually wins. Village panchayats make local rules too.

Laws can change daily life. The [[@right-to-information|Right to Information Act]] of 2005 lets any citizen ask government offices for information. The Right to Education Act of 2009, part of India's laws on [[@rights-kids|children's rights]], promises free schooling to children aged 6 to 14. If a law goes too far, the [[@supreme-courts|Supreme Court]] can step in, as it has many times since 1950.

text: जब तुम कुछ सीखते हो, तो दिमाग की कोशिकाएँ, जिन्हें [[neuron|न्यूरॉन]] कहते हैं, आपस में अपने जुड़ाव मज़बूत करती हैं। हर बार किसी तथ्य या हुनर का इस्तेमाल करने पर वह रास्ता थोड़ा और आसान हो जाता है। एक तरह से सीखना यानी दिमाग में सड़कें बनाना।

वैज्ञानिकों ने पढ़ाई के बहुत-से तरीके परखे हैं। कुछ तरीके बार-बार अव्वल आते हैं: कई दिनों में फैलाकर अभ्यास करना, दोबारा पढ़ने के बजाय खुद का टेस्ट लेना, अलग-अलग तरह के सवाल मिलाकर करना, और पूरी नींद लेना। इनमें से किसी के लिए महँगे साधन नहीं चाहिए। हाँ, थोड़ी योजना लगती है, और ये अक्सर उन तरीकों से ज़्यादा मुश्किल लगते हैं जो उतने अच्छे से काम नहीं करते।

बहुत लोगों की अपनी पसंद होती है, पर सावधानी से की गई जाँचों में इसका कोई ठोस सबूत नहीं मिला कि पाठ को किसी "शैली" से मिलाने पर लोग ज़्यादा सीखते हैं। ज़्यादातर लोग तब सबसे अच्छा सीखते हैं जब बात कई रूपों में आए, जैसे शब्द, चित्र और अभ्यास, सब साथ-साथ।

sec.t:
1880 के दशक में हरमन एबिंगहॉस याददाश्त को मतलब की मदद के बिना मापना चाहते थे। तो उन्होंने गढ़े हुए, बेमतलब [[syllable|शब्दांशों]] की लंबी सूचियाँ याद कीं, और फिर मिनटों, घंटों और दिनों बाद खुद को परखा। उन्होंने पाया कि शुरू में हम बहुत तेज़ी से भूलते हैं। नई सूची का बड़ा हिस्सा एक दिन के अंदर ग़ायब हो जाता, और फिर भूलने की रफ़्तार धीमी पड़ जाती।

इलाज भी उन्होंने ही खोजा। हर बार किसी सूची को दोबारा सीखने में कम मेहनत लगती, और वह बाद में ज़्यादा देर तक टिकती। दोहराने के सत्रों के बीच फ़ासला रखने से वक्र चपटा हो गया। टीचर और ऐप बनाने वाले आज भी इस विचार का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जिसे स्पेस्ड रिपीटिशन कहते हैं, ताकि [[@multiplication-tables|पहाड़ों]], वर्तनी और नए शब्दों का अभ्यास सोच-समझकर हो।

sec.h: परखने से यादें पक्की होती हैं
sec.t:
ज़्यादातर छात्र नोट्स दोबारा पढ़कर पढ़ाई करते हैं। यह आरामदेह लगता है, क्योंकि शब्द जाने-पहचाने दिखते हैं। पर किसी चीज़ को पहचान लेना और उसे याद कर पाना एक बात नहीं है।

मनोवैज्ञानिकों ने ऐसे बहुत-से प्रयोग किए हैं जिनमें एक समूह कोई पाठ दोबारा पढ़ता है, और दूसरा समूह उसे एक बार पढ़कर जितना याद है सब लिखने की कोशिश करता है। एक हफ़्ते बाद दूसरे समूह को आम तौर पर कहीं ज़्यादा याद रहता है। किसी तथ्य को [[@memory|याददाश्त]] से खींचकर निकालना उसे मज़बूत करता है, कुछ वैसे ही जैसे पगडंडी जितनी ज़्यादा चलो, उतनी साफ़ होती जाती है। फ़्लैशकार्ड, अभ्यास के सवाल और किसी दोस्त को कोई बात समझाना, ये सब इसी में गिने जाते हैं।

पढ़ाना खास तौर पर बढ़िया काम करता है। छोटे चचेरे भाई को [[photosynthesis|प्रकाश संश्लेषण]] समझाने के लिए तुम्हें बात को सिलसिलेवार जमाना होगा, आसान शब्द ढूँढने होंगे, और यह भी पकड़ना होगा कि कौन-सा हिस्सा तुम्हें खुद ठीक से समझ नहीं आया। बहुत-से टीचर कहते हैं कि कोई विषय उन्होंने असल में तभी सीखा जब उसे पढ़ाना पड़ा।

गणित का अभ्यास करते समय एक ही तरह के बीस सवाल एक के बाद एक करने का मन करता है। जाँचें बताती हैं कि अलग-अलग तरह के सवाल मिलाकर करना बेहतर है। इसे इंटरलीविंग कहते हैं। यह धीमा लगता है, क्योंकि हर सवाल पर सोचना पड़ता है कि कौन-सा तरीका लगेगा। यही फ़ालतू सोच असली टेस्ट में काम आती है, जहाँ सवाल किसी भी क्रम में आ सकते हैं।

यही बात खेल और संगीत पर भी लागू होती है। क्रिकेट के बहुत-से कोच नेट प्रैक्टिस में तेज़, धीमी और स्पिन गेंदें मिलाकर डलवाते हैं, ताकि बल्लेबाज़ अंदाज़ा लगाने के बजाय गेंदबाज़ को पढ़ना सीखें।

sec.h: नींद भी पढ़ाई का हिस्सा है
sec.t:
सोते समय दिमाग दिन के कुछ अनुभवों को दोबारा चलाता है। इससे नई यादें लंबे समय के भंडार में पहुँचती हैं। जो छात्र पूरी रात जागकर रटते हैं, उन्हें अक्सर उन छात्रों से कम याद रहता है जो पढ़कर पूरी रात की [[@sleep-why|नींद]] लेते हैं।

झपकी भी मदद कर सकती है, खासकर छोटे बच्चों के लिए। और कसरत से दिमाग तक ज़्यादा खून पहुँचता है, जिससे लोग ज़्यादा चुस्त और सीखने के लिए तैयार महसूस करते हैं।

पढ़ाई के बहुत-से अच्छे तरीके असहज लगते हैं। खुद को परखने से पता चलता है कि तुम्हें क्या नहीं आता, जो अच्छा नहीं लगता। सवाल मिलाकर करना उलझा-उलझा लगता है। मनोवैज्ञानिक इन्हें "काम की मुश्किलें" कहते हैं। यह मेहनत इस बात का संकेत है कि दिमाग कुछ बना रहा है।

इसीलिए [[@learning-languages|नई भाषा]] या कोई वाद्य सीखते समय बीच-बीच में धीमे दौर आते हैं। अटकना, गलती करना और फिर कोशिश करना इस बात की निशानी नहीं कि तुम इसमें कमज़ोर हो। दिमाग की सड़कें ऐसे ही बनती हैं।

text: प्रत्यारोपण में सर्जन एक इंसान, यानी दानदाता, से एक सेहतमंद [[organ|अंग]] निकालकर ऐसे इंसान में लगाते हैं जिसका अपना अंग काम करना बंद कर चुका है। गुर्दे, लिवर, दिल, फेफड़े, अग्न्याशय और आँख का [[cornea|कॉर्निया]], सबका प्रत्यारोपण हो सकता है।

ऑपरेशन अपने आप में कठिन है, पर मुमकिन है। बड़ी चुनौती है [[@immune-system|प्रतिरक्षा तंत्र]], जो शरीर की रक्षा करने वाली सेना है। यह हर उस चीज़ पर हमला करता है जिसे वह पराया समझता है, दान में मिले अंग पर भी। इसलिए डॉक्टर दानदाता और मरीज़ का मिलान जितना हो सके उतना क़रीबी करते हैं, और मरीज़ बाद में दवाएँ लेते हैं ताकि शरीर नए अंग को ठुकरा न दे।

sec.t:
बरसों तक डॉक्टरों ने गुर्दे बदलने की कोशिश की, पर मरीज़ों के शरीर हर बार उन्हें ठुकरा देते। फिर 1954 में अमेरिका के बोस्टन में रिचर्ड हेरिक नाम का एक नौजवान गुर्दे ख़राब होने से मौत के क़रीब था। उसका एक हूबहू जुड़वाँ भाई था, रोनाल्ड।

हूबहू जुड़वाँ के [[gene|जीन]] एक जैसे होते हैं, इसलिए सर्जन जोसेफ़ मरे ने सोचा कि शायद रिचर्ड का शरीर रोनाल्ड का गुर्दा अपना ले। 23 दिसंबर 1954 को उन्होंने गुर्दा लगा दिया। यह काम कर गया, और रिचर्ड आठ साल और जिए। रोनाल्ड ने सिर्फ़ एक गुर्दे के साथ लंबी ज़िंदगी जी। इस काम के लिए मरे को 1990 में नोबेल पुरस्कार मिला।

कुछ अंग किसी ज़िंदा इंसान से भी आ सकते हैं। तुम्हारे दो [[@kidneys|गुर्दे]] हैं, पर तुम एक के साथ भी अच्छे से जी सकते हो। इसलिए माता-पिता, भाई-बहन और पति-पत्नी अक्सर गुर्दा दान करते हैं। लिवर का एक हिस्सा भी दिया जा सकता है, क्योंकि वह फिर से बढ़ जाता है।

सबसे पुराने प्रत्यारोपणों में से एक है कॉर्निया का, जो आँख के सामने की पारदर्शी खिड़की है। पहला कामयाब कॉर्निया प्रत्यारोपण 1905 में एडुआर्ड ज़िर्म ने किया, उस जगह जो आज चेक गणराज्य है। कॉर्निया में खून की नलियाँ नहीं होतीं, इसलिए प्रतिरक्षा तंत्र उस पर शायद ही कभी हमला करता है। मौत के कुछ घंटों के अंदर इसे दान किया जा सकता है, घर पर भी, और पूरे भारत में आई बैंक इन्हें इकट्ठा करके लोगों की आँखों की रोशनी लौटाते हैं।

दिल, फेफड़े और ज़्यादातर दूसरे अंग उन लोगों से आते हैं जिनकी मौत हो चुकी है, आमतौर पर अस्पताल में ब्रेन डेथ के बाद, जब मशीनें अब भी उनका खून बहा रही होती हैं। परिवार की सहमति से ऐसा एक दानदाता आठ जानें तक बचा सकता है। भारत के शहरों में कभी-कभी पुलिस ट्रैफ़िक के बीच "ग्रीन कॉरिडोर" बनाती है, ताकि दान में मिला दिल ले जा रही एम्बुलेंस कुछ ही मिनटों में शहर पार कर ले। रफ़्तार मायने रखती है, क्योंकि शरीर के बाहर दिल बस लगभग चार से छह घंटे टिकता है।

2024 में भारत में 18,900 से ज़्यादा प्रत्यारोपण हुए, जो एक रिकॉर्ड है और दुनिया की सबसे बड़ी गिनतियों में से एक। फिर भी ज़रूरत वाले लोग कहीं ज़्यादा हैं। भारत में दान किए गए ज़्यादातर गुर्दे और लिवर ज़िंदा रिश्तेदारों से आते हैं, और स्पेन या अमेरिका जैसे देशों के मुकाबले यहाँ मौत के बाद अंगदान अब भी कम है। भारत का 1994 का प्रत्यारोपण क़ानून अंगों को ख़रीदने या बेचने को अपराध बनाता है।

मदद के लिए डॉक्टर नए स्रोत खोज रहे हैं। 2024 में बोस्टन के सर्जनों ने एक ज़िंदा आदमी को ऐसे सूअर का गुर्दा लगाया, जिसके जीन बदलकर उसे इंसानी शरीर के ज़्यादा अनुकूल बनाया गया था। दूसरी टीमें प्रयोगशालाओं में अंगों जैसे नन्हे ऊतक उगा रही हैं। तब तक सबसे सीधी मदद उन लोगों से आती है जो [[@organ-donation|अंगदान]] करने का फ़ैसला करते हैं और अपने परिवार को बताते हैं, ताकि उनकी इच्छा पूरी की जा सके।

text: [[@future-cities|In 2050]], most people will probably still walk, cycle, take buses and trains, and drive cars. The big change is likely to be what powers them. Many countries plan for most new cars, scooters and buses to be [[@electric-cars|electric]] well before then, and for faster trains to link big cities.

A few bolder ideas, such as flying taxis and self-driving cars, are being tested now. Some may become common. Others may turn out like the [[@flying-cars|flying cars]] of 1950s magazines: always about ten years away. The honest answer is that engineers know what they're building, but nobody knows which ideas people will actually use.

st.prompt: Which of these is most likely to carry the most people around Indian and American cities in 2050?

options.t: Trains, metros and electric buses
Flying taxis
Hyperloop pods

st.reveal: Flying taxis and hyperloops may carry a few people, but they are expensive and carry small loads. A single metro train can move over a thousand passengers at once, so most transport experts expect mass transit to do the heavy lifting.

n.certNote: Nobody can know the future. Some technologies, such as electric vehicles and high-speed rail, are already spreading fast. Others, such as hyperloops and flying taxis, may or may not become common, and experts disagree about which will win.

myth: Electric cars cause no pollution at all.

Electric cars have no exhaust pipe, so they don't pollute the street. But making their batteries uses energy and mining, and the electricity they use may come from coal. Their tyres and brakes also shed dust.

sec.t:
Transport burns a lot of fuel. Cars, trucks, ships and planes produce roughly a fifth of the world's energy-related [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]], the main gas behind [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Exhaust fumes also make city air harder to breathe, from Delhi to Los Angeles.

So most plans for 2050 aim at two things: cleaner power and fewer cars per person. That's why you'll hear about batteries, hydrogen, metro lines and cycle lanes all at once.

Long-distance trucks, ships and planes are harder. Batteries heavy enough to [[@electric-planes|fly a jumbo jet]] across an ocean would weigh too much. Engineers are testing [[@hydrogen-fuel|hydrogen]], fuels made from plants or waste, and more efficient engines. These are likely to arrive more slowly than [[@ev-charging|electric cars]], and may still be rare in 2050.

{{story:climate-change}}

India's first bullet train line is being built between Mumbai and [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]], about 508 km. It is designed for speeds of up to 320 km/h, which would cut the trip to around two or three hours. In the US, California has been building a high-speed line for years, though it has faced long delays and rising costs.

Japan is going further with a [[@maglev|maglev]] line, where trains float on magnets. A test train reached 603 km/h in 2015, faster than a small plane. The full line from Tokyo to Nagoya has been delayed, and won't open before the 2030s.

sec.h: Ideas still on the drawing board
sec.t:
A [[@hyperloop|hyperloop]] would shoot pods through tubes with most of the air pumped out, at airliner speeds. It got huge attention in the 2010s, and India even studied a Mumbai to Pune route. But building long, airtight tubes is very expensive, and in 2023 Hyperloop One, the best-funded company, closed down.

Flying taxis are small electric aircraft that take off straight up, like a helicopter, but quieter. Several companies are testing them, and a few cities hope to start short routes soon. They may end up as an expensive option for [[@airports|airports]] and traffic-jammed business districts, not something most families use daily. They also need new rules for crowded skies, and places to land on rooftops.

[[@self-driving|Self-driving cars]] already carry paying passengers in a few US cities, such as San Francisco and Phoenix. They still struggle with unusual roads, and Indian traffic, with its cows, handcarts and autorickshaws, is a tougher test than a neat American grid.

Some of the biggest changes may look ordinary. Electric two-wheelers and three-wheelers are spreading fast in India. Cities are adding metro lines, bus lanes and bicycle paths. Parcels may arrive by small [[@drones-delivery|drones]] in some places.

The child who rides a metro to school in 2050 might not find it futuristic at all. Their grandparents, who rode a crowded bus on a dusty road, would see it very differently.

text: The Persian Empire, also called the Achaemenid Empire, was founded by Cyrus the Great around 550 BCE in what is now Iran. Within a few decades it became the largest [[empire|empire]] the world had yet seen. At its height under Darius I, it stretched from Egypt and the edge of Greece in the west to the Indus river in the east.

The Persians ruled dozens of different peoples by dividing the empire into provinces called satrapies, each under a governor. They built a long royal road and a fast postal service, and often let local people keep their own gods and customs. The empire lasted until Alexander the Great conquered it in 330 BCE.

st.prompt: How long did it take a royal messenger, riding in relays, to cover the Persian Royal Road of about 2,500 km?

options.t: About a week to ten days
About two days
About three months

st.reveal: Travellers on foot took around three months, but royal messengers swapped to fresh horses at stations along the way and are thought to have covered it in about a week or so. It was one of the fastest communication systems of the ancient world.

myth: The ancient Persians were simply the villains of Greek history.

Most of the stories come from their Greek enemies. Persian records show a well-organised empire that built roads, ran a postal system, and often let conquered peoples keep their own customs and religions.

sec.t:
Cyrus began as the ruler of a small kingdom in southern Iran. He defeated the Medes, then the rich kingdom of Lydia in Turkey, and in 539 BCE he took Babylon, the great city of [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]].

A clay cylinder found in Babylon in 1879, now in the British Museum, records his conquest. It says he restored temples and let peoples who had been taken from their homes return. The Hebrew Bible praises Cyrus for allowing the Jews exiled in Babylon to go back to [[@jerusalem|Jerusalem]]. A copy of the Cyrus Cylinder is displayed at the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] headquarters in New York.

The empire reached into the Indus region, in today's Pakistan. Herodotus said this Indian province paid more tribute than any other, in gold dust. Indian soldiers served in Persian armies, and carvings at Persepolis show Indians bringing gifts.

Persian rule left traces in India. The Kharosthi script, used in the northwest for centuries, is thought to have grown out of Aramaic, the language of Persian government offices. Some historians also see Persian influence in the polished stone pillars of the Mauryan emperor [[@ashoka|Ashoka]], built about two centuries later.

Much of Iran is dry. Persians became experts at building qanats, underground tunnels that carry water from mountain springs to villages and fields far away, without losing it to the sun. Some qanats run for tens of kilometres, and many are still in use. UNESCO lists a group of Persian qanats as a World Heritage Site.

The Persians were also known for the religion of Zoroastrianism, which spoke of a struggle between truth and falsehood. Centuries later, Zoroastrians who left Iran settled in Gujarat. Their [[descendant|descendants]] are India's Parsi community.

sec.h: Wars with Greece and the end
sec.t:
Darius and his son Xerxes tried to conquer Greece. The Greeks beat them at [[@running-marathon|Marathon]] in 490 BCE, and again at Salamis and Plataea in 480 and 479 BCE. These wars made heroes of the Greek city-states in their own histories.

In 334 BCE, [[@alexander-india|Alexander]] of Macedon invaded. He defeated the last Persian king, Darius III, and in 330 BCE Persepolis was burned. Its ruined columns still stand on a terrace in southern Iran, a World Heritage Site where visitors can see the carved gift-bearers climbing the stairs.

text: George Washington led the American army that won independence from Britain, and then became the [[@usa-presidents-facts|first President of the United States]]. Americans often call him the "Father of His Country".

He was not a brilliant general who won every battle. He lost quite a few. But he kept a ragged army together through eight hard years and never gave up. After winning, he did something rulers rarely do: he gave power back. He resigned from the army in 1783, and as president he stepped down after two terms. That habit of leaving office peacefully became one of the foundations of American [[@democracy-what|democracy]].

st.prompt: On the night of 25 December 1776, Washington's tired army made a surprise attack. How did they reach the enemy?

options.t: By crossing an icy river in boats in the dark
By riding a new railway line
By marching through a tunnel

st.reveal: Washington's soldiers crossed the Delaware River through floating ice and sleet, then marched to Trenton, New Jersey. They captured about 900 enemy soldiers. The win came when many Americans thought the war was lost.

myth: Young George chopped down a cherry tree and said, "I cannot tell a lie."
The story was invented by an author called Mason Locke Weems, who added it to his book about Washington in 1806, after Washington had died. There is no evidence it happened.

sec.t:
Washington was born in 1732 in Virginia, then a British colony. His father died when he was 11, so he never went to university. As a teenager he worked as a surveyor, measuring and mapping land in the wild country to the west. It taught him to travel, read landscapes and live rough. He kept careful notebooks of measurements, a habit of record-keeping he never lost. As a boy he also copied out 110 rules of good manners, about how to behave politely at the table and in company.

At 21 he joined the Virginia militia and fought for Britain against the French. He was tall, around 1.88 m, and calm under fire.

When the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]] began in 1775, Congress chose Washington to command its army. His soldiers were farmers, shopkeepers and boys, often without proper uniforms or boots.

The darkest time came in late 1776. The army had lost New York and was shrinking. On [[@christmas|Christmas]] night, Washington led his men across the icy Delaware River and surprised an enemy camp at Trenton. The win gave the army fresh hope. The war ended with victory at Yorktown in 1781.

In 1787 Washington chaired the [[@usa-wonder-philadelphia|meeting in Philadelphia]] that wrote the [[@us-constitution|US Constitution]]. Two years later he was elected the first president. He remains the only president to win every single electoral vote, and he did it twice.

He was sworn in on 30 April 1789 in New York City, the capital at the time. Everything he did set an example, even what to call the president. Some people suggested grand titles. He accepted the plain "Mr. President".

In 1796 Washington announced he would not run for a third term. He went back to Mount Vernon, his farm by the Potomac River. Presidents followed his two-term custom for nearly 150 years, and in 1951 it became law.

Washington's life had a hard side too. Mount Vernon ran on the labour of enslaved people. More than 300 were living there when he died. In his will, he ordered that the people he personally owned be freed after his wife Martha's death. Martha freed them in 1801.

text: Women have shaped India's story for thousands of years, as rulers, warriors, thinkers, poets, teachers, doctors and freedom fighters. Many are famous, like [[@rani-lakshmibai|Rani Lakshmibai]] of Jhansi. Others are less well known outside their own regions.

Here are a few of them. You will meet a sultan in Delhi, a queen in central India, a teacher in Pune, a doctor who studied in America, and the women who helped write India's [[constitution|constitution]]. Each one did something people around her said a woman could not do.

st.prompt: When Savitribai Phule walked to the girls' school where she taught in the 1840s, some people threw mud and stones at her. What did she do about it?

options.t: She stopped teaching and stayed home
She carried a spare sari and changed when she reached school
She moved the school to a secret cave

st.reveal: Many people at the time believed girls, especially from poorer and lower-caste families, should not be educated. Savitribai is remembered for carrying a second sari so she could change and teach in clean clothes, and for never giving up.

myth: Women played little part in India's history until modern times.
Women ruled kingdoms, led armies, wrote poetry, debated philosophy and ran trade for many centuries. Their stories were often written down less, so historians have to look harder to find them.

sec.t:
The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad is one of India's ancient texts. In it, a woman scholar named Gargi asks the sage Yajnavalkya question after question about the nature of the universe, in front of a king's court. She is remembered as a sharp and fearless thinker.

Centuries later, in 1236, Razia became ruler of the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. Her father, Iltutmish, chose her over her brothers. Razia dressed like a male ruler, held court in public and rode an elephant into battle. Some nobles disliked being ruled by a woman, and she was overthrown and killed in 1240. She was the only woman to rule from the throne of Delhi in the sultanate era.

sec.h: The teacher who would not quit
sec.t:
In 1848 Savitribai [[@jyotirao-phule|Phule]] and her husband, Jyotirao Phule, opened a school for girls in Pune. At that time, very few girls in India went to school, and education for girls from lower castes was fiercely opposed. Savitribai became one of India's first women teachers.

She went on to open more schools, care for widows and orphans, and write poetry. In 1897, while nursing people during a plague outbreak, she caught the disease herself and died. Her birthday, 3 January, is marked in Maharashtra as a day to honour women's education.

Anandibai Joshi, born near Kalyan in Maharashtra, lost a baby son when she was 14, partly because good medical care was not available. She decided to become a doctor. In 1883 she sailed to the United States and studied at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania. She graduated in 1886, one of the first Indian women to earn a degree in Western medicine.

She returned to India to lead the women's ward of a hospital in Kolhapur, but she had fallen ill with [[@tb-india|tuberculosis]]. She died in 1887, aged just 21.

When India's [[@constituent-assembly|Constituent Assembly]] met to write the constitution, 15 of its members were women. They included [[@sarojini-naidu|Sarojini Naidu]], poet and freedom fighter; Hansa Mehta, who later helped write the [[@human-rights|Universal Declaration of Human Rights]]; and Dakshayani Velayudhan, the only Dalit woman in the Assembly. Thanks partly to them, the constitution gave every adult woman the vote from the very start in 1950, something many older [[democracy|democracies]] had taken decades to do.

text: Petra is an ancient city in southern Jordan, carved straight into cliffs of reddish sandstone. It was built by the Nabataeans, a wealthy Arab trading people, who made it their capital more than 2,000 years ago.

The Nabataeans did not build most of Petra's grand buildings out of blocks. They cut them out of the solid rock face, like sculptors carving a statue. Using iron chisels and hammers, stonecutters started at the top of a cliff and worked down, shaping columns, doorways and decorations as they went. Behind each grand front, they hollowed out rooms. Hundreds of tombs, temples and halls fill the valley, glowing pink, orange and red in the sunlight.

st.prompt: To carve the Treasury's tall front out of a cliff, where did the Nabataean stonecutters most likely begin?

options.t: At the top, cutting downwards
At the bottom, cutting upwards
In the middle, working outwards

st.reveal: Starting at the top meant workers could stand on the uncut rock beneath them, so they needed little scaffolding. Unfinished tombs at Petra show this, with finished tops and rough, uncut lower parts.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Petra.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Petra.
n.certNote: Archaeologists agree on how the facades were carved, but they still debate what some buildings were for. The Treasury, for example, may have been a royal tomb or a temple.

myth: The Treasury at Petra was built to hold treasure.

It got its name from a later Bedouin legend that treasure was hidden in the stone urn at the top. People even shot at the urn to try to break it open. Archaeologists think the building was most likely a royal tomb.

sec.t:
Petra stood at a crossroads of desert [[@trade-routes|trade routes]]. Camel [[caravan|caravans]] carried frankincense and myrrh from southern Arabia, along with spices and silk from further east, towards the Mediterranean. The Nabataeans controlled the water and the paths, and they grew rich by charging and supplying the traders.

With that wealth, they built a city that may have held around 20,000 people at its peak. Their buildings mix styles from Egypt, Greece and [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], because traders brought ideas as well as goods.

Petra gets little rain, but when storms come, water rushes down the rocky gorges as flash [[@floods-why|floods]]. The Nabataeans turned this danger into a supply. They built dams to slow and redirect floods, channels cut into rock along the walls of the gorges, clay pipes and big underground cisterns to store water.

Some experts think this clever water system mattered as much as trade to Petra's success. It let the city grow gardens and fountains in a dry valley, much as [[@india-wonder-chand-baori|stepwells in Rajasthan]] and Gujarat kept water through the dry season.

The main way into Petra is the Siq, a narrow, winding gorge about 1.2 km long. Its walls rise up to about 80 m, and in places it is only a few metres wide. As you walk, the gorge curves and darkens, then suddenly opens to reveal the Treasury, glowing in the light.

That view appeared in the 1989 film Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, which made Petra famous around the world.

In 106 CE, the Roman Empire took over the kingdom, as told in [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]]. Trade routes shifted to the sea, and an earthquake in 363 CE damaged much of the city. Over time, most people left.

Local Bedouin families never forgot Petra and lived among its caves. But to Europeans it was a legend until 1812, when a Swiss traveller, Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, visited in disguise. In 2007 it was voted one of the new [[@seven-wonders|Seven Wonders]], and today [[@archaeology|archaeologists]] say most of the city still lies unexcavated.

text: The Serengeti is a huge stretch of grassland in northern Tanzania, in East Africa. Its name comes from a Maasai word meaning "endless plains". On a clear day, flat yellow grass seems to stretch all the way to the sky.

It is famous for the Great Migration. Wildebeest are a kind of antelope, though with their beards and big heads they look more like small cattle. Every year, around 1.3 to 1.5 million wildebeest, along with hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles, travel in a giant loop through the Serengeti and into Kenya's Maasai Mara. They follow the rains to find fresh grass. Lions, cheetahs, [[@wild-hyena|hyenas]] and crocodiles wait along the way.

st.prompt: What keeps more than a million wildebeest moving all year?

options.t: Following the rain and the fresh grass it brings
Escaping the lions that hunt them
Heading to the same river to drink every month

st.reveal: Rain falls in different parts of the Serengeti at different times of year. The herds move to wherever new grass is growing. Lions and other hunters follow the herds, not the other way round.

src: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Serengeti National Park.
Tanzania National Parks, Serengeti National Park.

n.certNote: The migration is real and well studied, but counting moving herds is hard. Estimates of the number of wildebeest usually range from about 1.3 to 1.5 million, depending on the year and the survey.

sec.t:
The most dramatic moment comes at the Mara River. Thousands of wildebeest gather on the bank, nervous and noisy. Then one jumps, and the rest pour after it in a rush of dust and splashing.

Huge Nile crocodiles wait in the brown water. Some animals are caught, and others are swept away by the current or trampled in the crush. Most make it across. Some herds cross the river several times in a season, heading back and forth as rain falls on one side or the other.

Zebras and wildebeest don't really compete. Zebras often go first and eat the tall, tough tops of the grass. Wildebeest then eat the shorter, leafier parts underneath, and gazelles nibble the fresh shoots that grow back. Each animal makes the grass better for the next.

The grassland is dotted with kopjes, piles of rounded [[granite|granite]] boulders sticking out of the plains. Lions rest on them in the heat and use them as lookouts. The whole [[@grasslands|grassland]] depends on a balance between rain, grass, grazers and hunters, and a long [[drought|drought]] can tip it fast.

In the 1950s and early 1960s, the wildebeest population was only about a quarter of a million. A cattle disease called rinderpest was killing many calves. Then vets began vaccinating cattle around the park, which stopped the disease spreading. Within about twenty years, wildebeest numbers had grown to well over a million. It's one of the clearest examples of [[@vaccines|vaccines]] protecting wild animals as well as farm ones.

In 1959, a German father and son, Bernhard and Michael Grzimek, made a film called Serengeti Shall Not Die, which won an Oscar. Michael was killed during the filming when a vulture struck his small plane. The film made the park famous around the world.

Today, people still argue about how to share the land around the park between wildlife, farmers and Maasai herders, whose cattle have grazed these plains for centuries. Roads, fences and farms on the edges could block the herds' path. The wildebeest ignore the border between Tanzania and Kenya. So the Serengeti and the Maasai Mara, the heart of many a [[@kenya-safari|safari in Kenya]], have to be protected together, as one great loop of grass.

text: Japanese uses three scripts because it borrowed one and then invented two more to fit its own language.

About 1,500 years ago, Japan had no writing of its own. It borrowed Chinese characters, which the Japanese call kanji. But Japanese grammar is very different from Chinese. Japanese words change their endings to show things like tense, and the language uses small grammar words that Chinese doesn't have. Kanji were clumsy for that.

So Japanese writers simplified some kanji into quick sound symbols, called kana. Over time these became two sets: rounded hiragana and angular katakana. Today kanji carry the main meaning of words, hiragana handle grammar endings and little words, and katakana are used mostly for foreign words and [[@words-onomatopoeia|sound effects]].

st.prompt: Japanese has a special script, katakana, used mainly for one kind of word. Which kind?

options.t: Words borrowed from other languages, like "television"
The names of the emperor's family
Words only used by grandparents

st.reveal: Katakana is mostly used for words from abroad, such as テレビ (terebi, television) and アイスクリーム (aisukurīmu, ice cream). It is also used for sound effects in manga, a bit like writing "BOOM" in capital letters.

d.try: Find a manga or a Japanese product label at home or in a library. Look for three kinds of writing. Kanji look busy and squarish, hiragana are soft and curvy, and katakana are sharp and angular. Count how many of each you can spot on one page.
myth: Japanese is a dialect of Chinese, because it uses Chinese characters.

Japanese and Chinese are unrelated languages with very different grammar and sounds. Japan borrowed Chinese characters long ago, the way English borrowed the Latin alphabet, and then built its own scripts too.

sec.t:
Take the sentence 私はアイスクリームを食べます, "I eat ice cream". 私 (I) and 食 (eat) are kanji. は, を and べます are hiragana, doing the grammar work. アイスクリーム, *aisukurīmu*, is katakana for the borrowed English word "ice cream".

Mixing scripts helps readers. Japanese is usually written without spaces between words, so the switch from kanji to hiragana shows where one word ends and the grammar begins. It works like a built-in highlighter.

Many kanji can be read in more than one way. 生 can be *sei*, *shō*, *nama* or *i(kiru)*, depending on the word. Books for young readers print tiny hiragana beside hard kanji to show how to say them. These helpers are called furigana.

There is even a fourth set of symbols in daily use: rōmaji, the Roman letters of English. You see them in company names, on station signs for visitors, and when people type. Most Japanese people type by spelling words out in Roman letters on a keyboard, and the computer turns them into kana and kanji.

sec.h: The women who wrote in kana
sec.t:
In the 800s and 900s, men at the Japanese court were expected to write formal Chinese. Hiragana was seen as less serious and was used widely by women. Women writers used it to produce some of the greatest books in Japanese.

Around the early 1000s, a court lady known as Murasaki Shikibu wrote *The Tale of Genji*, a long story about life at the emperor's court in what is now [[@kyoto|Kyoto]]. It is often called one of the world's first novels. It was written mostly in hiragana, the script men looked down on.

The Japanese government keeps an official list of 2,136 kanji for everyday use, last updated in 2010. Children learn about a thousand of them in primary school and the rest in secondary school.

They also learn all 46 basic hiragana and 46 katakana, usually in their first year. Hiragana come first, so a six-year-old can write any word in hiragana even before learning its kanji. Japanese students also practise brush writing, called *shodō*, a form of [[@calligraphy|calligraphy]].

Traditionally, Japanese was written in vertical columns, from top to bottom, starting on the right. Many novels and newspapers still are, and so are many manga, which are read from what an English reader would call the back of the book. Textbooks on maths and science, and most websites, use horizontal lines from left to right instead.

Japanese writing has also given the world new words. "[[@words-emoji-language|Emoji]]" is Japanese for "picture character". The first popular set of emoji was designed for Japanese mobile phones in 1999, before they spread worldwide as [[@emojis|emojis]] on every phone.

text: Millets are [[@grains-world|small, hardy grains]] such as ragi (finger millet), jowar (sorghum) and bajra (pearl millet). For thousands of years they were staple foods across dry parts of India and Africa, because they grow in heat and poor soil with little water.

After the 1960s, rice and wheat took over many farms and kitchens, and millets came to be seen as old-fashioned. Now they are returning. Farmers like that they survive [[drought|droughts]], doctors like their fibre and minerals, and the government has campaigned to bring them back to everyday meals.

st.prompt: Which of these grains has the most calcium, the mineral that builds strong bones?

options.t: Ragi
White rice
Wheat

st.reveal: Ragi, or finger millet, has over 300 mg of calcium in every 100 g, according to India's National Institute of Nutrition. White rice has only about 10 mg. That is why ragi porridge is a traditional first food for babies in Karnataka.

src: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), International Year of Millets 2023.
ICRISAT (International Crops Research Institute for the Semi-Arid Tropics), millets.
ICMR National Institute of Nutrition, Indian Food Composition Tables (2017).
n.certNote: Millets are clearly hardy crops and good sources of fibre and minerals. Some popular health claims, such as millets curing diabetes, go further than the scientific evidence.

d.try: Soak a spoon of ragi or bajra in water overnight. Next morning, drain it and wrap it in a damp cloth. Keep the cloth moist and check every day. In two or three days you should see tiny white sprouts.
myth: Millets are just bird seed.
In the United States, millet is best known in bird feeders. But in India and much of Africa, millets are everyday food for hundreds of millions of people, eaten as rotis, porridge, dosas and more.

sec.t:
Millet grains have been found at Harappan sites, the cities of the [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley]]. Ragi probably came to India from the highlands of East Africa around 4,000 years ago and became a favourite in the south.

Every region has its millet dish. Karnataka has ragi mudde, a soft ball dipped in sambar. Maharashtra has jowar bhakri, a thick flatbread. Rajasthan eats bajra rotis with garlic chutney, and the hills of [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]] have mandua rotis made from ragi.

In the 1960s India faced food shortages. The [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]] brought new high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, with fertilisers and [[irrigation|irrigation]]. Harvests grew enormously and [[famine|famines]] ended.

But government support, cheap ration grain and city tastes all favoured rice and wheat. Millets started to look like "poor people's food". Over the following decades the area of land growing millets in India shrank a great deal, and many families switched from bajra [[@roti-chapati|rotis]] to wheat chapatis.

India proposed, and the [[@united-nations|United Nations]] declared, 2023 the International Year of Millets. The Indian government began calling them Shree Anna, and some states added ragi and jowar to school meals and ration shops.

Millets are rich in fibre and minerals such as iron and magnesium, and ragi is unusually high in [[@bones-growth|calcium]]. They are also gluten-free, which helps people who cannot eat wheat. Still, scientists warn that millets are good food, not medicine. Some claims on packets go further than the evidence.

Millets can be tricky in the kitchen, which is one reason they fell out of favour in busy city homes. Millet flour has no [[gluten|gluten]], so a bajra roti cannot stretch like a wheat chapati. Cooks pat it out by hand on a wet cloth or between their palms, and it cracks easily.

New recipes are helping. Shops now sell ragi dosa mix, jowar flakes, millet noodles and even millet biscuits. Some cooks simply swap half the rice in a pulao or khichdi for foxtail millet. Old grains, it turns out, can fit into new routines.

In the United States, millets are mostly a farm crop. Kansas is the biggest grower of sorghum, much of which feeds cattle or is turned into fuel. Proso millet fills bird feeders across the country. A few American bakers and chefs now use sorghum flour, often learning recipes from Indian and African cooks who never stopped.

text: आलू की खेती सबसे पहले दक्षिण अमेरिका के [[@peru|एंडीज़]] पहाड़ों में हुई, पेरू और बोलीविया की सीमा पर टिटिकाका झील के पास, लगभग 8,000 साल पहले। वहाँ के किसान आलू की सैकड़ों क़िस्में उगाते थे, पीले से लेकर गहरे बैंगनी तक हर रंग की।

1500 के दशक में स्पेन के विजेता आलू को अटलांटिक पार यूरोप ले गए। अगले 300 सालों में आलू स्पेन से आयरलैंड, रूस, भारत और चीन तक फैल गया। एक खेत में यह गेहूँ से ज़्यादा खाना देता था, ठंडी जगहों पर उग जाता था, और ज़रूरत पड़ने पर ही खोदकर निकाला जा सकता था। आज यह दुनिया की सबसे अहम खाद्य फ़सलों में से एक है, और सबसे ज़्यादा आलू चीन और भारत उगाते हैं।

sec.t:
शुरू में बहुत-से यूरोपीय लोग आलू पर भरोसा नहीं करते थे। यह ज़मीन के नीचे से निकला एक अजीब-सा ढेला था, ज़हरीले नाइटशेड पौधों का रिश्तेदार, और इसके हरे हिस्से सच में ज़हरीले होते हैं। कुछ लोग सोचते थे कि इससे बीमारी होती है।

राजाओं को इसके लिए ज़ोर लगाना पड़ा। 1700 के दशक में प्रशा के राजा फ़्रेडरिक महान ने किसानों को हुक्म दिया कि [[famine|अकाल]] से बचने के लिए आलू उगाओ। फ़्रांस में वैज्ञानिक आंत्वान-ऑगस्तें पारमांतिए ने, जिन्होंने युद्धबंदी रहते हुए आलू खाए थे, इसके पक्ष में मुहिम चलाई। धीरे-धीरे जर्मनी से रूस तक आलू रोज़ का खाना बन गया।

आयरलैंड में कई ग़रीब परिवार लगभग पूरी तरह आलू पर ही निर्भर हो गए थे। 1845 में पोटैटो ब्लाइट नाम की एक बीमारी आई। इसने पौधों को काला कर दिया और ज़मीन के अंदर ही आलू सड़ा दिए।

कई साल लगातार फ़सल बर्बाद हुई। 1845 से 1852 के बीच लगभग दस लाख लोग मारे गए, और लगभग दस लाख और लोग आयरलैंड छोड़कर चले गए, जिनमें से बहुत-से जहाज़ से अमेरिका पहुँचे। इसी वजह से आज करोड़ों अमेरिकियों के पुरखे आयरलैंड के हैं। यह उन [[@immigration-stories|प्रवास की कहानियों]] का हिस्सा है जिन्होंने उस देश को गढ़ा। वैज्ञानिक अब जानते हैं कि ब्लाइट फफूँद जैसे एक सूक्ष्मजीव से होता है, जो नमी वाले मौसम में फैलता है।

पुर्तगाली व्यापारी 1600 के दशक में आलू भारत लाए, शायद सबसे पहले पश्चिमी तट पर। बाद में अंग्रेज़ अफ़सरों ने इसे [[@himachal|शिमला]], दार्जिलिंग और नीलगिरि जैसे पहाड़ी इलाक़ों में लगाया, जहाँ का ठंडा मौसम इसे रास आया।

[[@hindi-language|हिंदी]] का शब्द *आलू* भारत में आलू के आने से भी पुराना है। पहले यह दूसरे कंदों और जड़ों के लिए इस्तेमाल होता था। आज आलू के बिना भारतीय खाने की कल्पना करना मुश्किल है: [[@indian-breakfasts|आलू का पराँठा]], दम आलू, वड़ा पाव और [[@samosa|समोसे]] की भरावन। भारत का राष्ट्रीय आलू अनुसंधान संस्थान 1949 में बना था और अब शिमला में है। भारत में सबसे ज़्यादा आलू उत्तर प्रदेश और पश्चिम बंगाल उगाते हैं।

आलू एक [[tuber|कंद]] है, यानी ज़मीन के नीचे वाले तने का फूला हुआ सिरा, जो [[starch|स्टार्च]] से भरा होता है। पौधा सर्दी काटने और बसंत में फिर से उगने के लिए वहाँ खाना जमा करता है।

तना होने की वजह से आलू रोशनी में पड़ा रहे तो हरा हो जाता है। हरा रंग तो बेनुक़सान [[chlorophyll|क्लोरोफ़िल]] का है, पर यह ख़तरे का इशारा है: हरे धब्बों में सोलानिन भी हो सकता है, जो एक कड़वा क़ुदरती ज़हर है। रसोइये हरे हिस्से काटकर फेंक देते हैं, और आलू को अँधेरे में रखना ही सबसे अच्छा है।

1995 में अमेरिका की विस्कॉन्सिन यूनिवर्सिटी के वैज्ञानिकों ने स्पेस शटल कोलंबिया के अंदर आलू के छोटे पौधे उगाए। अंतरिक्ष में कोई खाद्य पौधा पहली बार उगाया गया था। तब से अंतरिक्ष यात्री अंतरराष्ट्रीय [[@space-station|स्पेस स्टेशन]] पर लेट्यूस और दूसरी हरी पत्तियाँ भी उगा चुके हैं। इसके बारे में [[@space-food|अंतरिक्ष के खाने]] में पढ़ो।
